h1: The 6 Best Garden Augers for Potted Plants of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Garden Augers for Pots: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 garden augers for potted plants scored on bit diameter, length, drive size and build, from 9 inch to 36 inch.
summary: The Power Planter 7x28 gallon pot auger is the right tool for planting potted shrubs and perennials: a 7 inch bit that bores 28 inches deep and turns on a heavy 1/2 inch hex. The VASGOR three-piece set covers small pots, seedlings and bulbs with 1.6, 2.6 and 3.5 inch bits. The Power Planter 3x36 gives the longest reach, and the Insaga is the small starter-pot option.
intro: Digging a hole to fit a nursery pot sounds trivial until you do it twenty times. A shovel makes a wide, ragged hole, scatters soil across the bed and wears out your back. An auger bit chucked into a drill bores a clean cylinder the size of the pot, so the root ball drops straight in and the sides of the hole stay firm. That is the whole appeal.

But a bit that is too narrow forces you to enlarge each hole by hand, and a bit that is too wide leaves air gaps around the roots. We ranked six augers by matching bit diameter and length to the pot sizes people actually plant, then checked drive size, shaft construction and whether the listing says what drill you need.

products.name: Power Planter 7x28 Gallon Pot Auger
products.verdict: A 7 inch, 28 inch long auger sized for gallon pots, with a 1/2 inch hex drive.
products.description:
The Power Planter 7x28 pairs a 7 inch wide bit with double 10-gauge solid steel flighting, and it reaches 28 inches deep. The drive end is a 1/2 inch hex. That 7 inch width is sized to a gallon-pot root ball.

It ranks first because it is the only auger here built for gallon-size potted shrubs, trees and large perennials, which are the plants most gardeners actually buy. The 3x36 bores deeper but narrower, and the VASGOR set tops out at 3.5 inches, so neither can take a gallon pot.

Buy it for planting shrubs and large perennials. The caveat is the 1/2 inch drive: it needs a drill with a chuck that size, and a wide bit in clay will stall a weak drill.
products.idealFor: Gallon-size potted shrubs, trees and large perennials.
products.skipIf: You plant seedlings or have a light cordless drill.

products.name: VASGOR 3-Piece 16 Inch Auger Set
products.verdict: Three bits, 1.6, 2.6 and 3.5 inches wide, for small pots, seedlings and bulbs.
products.description:
VASGOR ships three 16 inch augers with 1.6, 2.6 and 3.5 inch bits, a solid shaft and a 3/8 inch hex drive, which fits the chuck on most cordless drills.

It ranks second because the three diameters match the range of small pots, from seedling cells to quart containers, without buying separate tools. It trails the Power Planter because 3.5 inches is the widest bit, which is too small for gallon pots.

Choose it for a mixed planting day of small pots, bulbs and seedlings. The caveat is the 16 inch length, which is short for deep planting, and the $25 to $50 price for three bits that each do one size.
pros: Three bit sizes in one set
products.idealFor: Mixed plantings of small pots, seedlings and bulbs.
products.skipIf: You plant gallon-size pots or need deep holes.

products.name: Power Planter 3x36 Bulb and Bedding Auger
products.verdict: A 36 inch, one-piece, hand-welded auger for standing planters who want reach.
products.description:
The Power Planter 3x36 is a hand-welded, one-piece auger with a 3 inch bit that runs 36 inches long. Its drive is a 1/2 inch non-slip hex. It is the longest auger ranked, and the one-piece weld has no joint to loosen.

It ranks third because 3 inches is only wide enough for bulbs and small plugs, not pots. The length is its asset: you can stand upright while planting, which spares your back. Next to the Jayzod, it is a simpler, cheaper build, though it does not come apart for storage.

Buy it for bulbs and bedding plants when you want to stay standing. The caveat is the 36 inch length, which is awkward to store.
products.idealFor: Standing planters putting in bulbs and bedding plants.
products.skipIf: You need to dig holes for larger pots.

products.name: Jayzod 34x3 Detachable Auger
products.verdict: A solid stainless shaft that separates for carrying, at a premium.
products.description:
Jayzod's 34x3 has a 3 inch bit and an assembled length of 34 inches, with a solid stainless steel shaft and a detachable design for carrying. It splits in two so it fits a tool bag.

It ranks fourth because its bit and reach match the Power Planter 3x36 for several times the price, in the $100 to $200 range. The detachable design is the reason to pay: a joint trades a little rigidity for portability, and stainless resists rust better than painted steel.

Buy it if you plant in several spots or have limited storage. The caveat is price, and the same narrow 3 inch bit that cannot take pots.
products.idealFor: Gardeners who plant in several spots or lack storage space.
products.skipIf: Price matters or you need a wide bit.

products.name: TCBWFY 3x24 Garden Auger
products.verdict: A simple 3 inch, 24 inch auger that wants an 18V drill, for quart pots and small shrubs.
products.description:
TCBWFY is a 3 inch by 24 inch auger with a 0.3 inch (8 mm) hex drive. The listing advises a drill of 18V or more and a chuck of 3/8 inch or larger.

It ranks fifth because it costs in the $100 to $200 bucket for a bit the Power Planter 3x36 matches for much less. The explicit drill advice is useful: a 3 inch bit in packed soil draws real torque, and a small cordless drill will stall.

Buy it for quart-size pots and small shrubs where you want depth in a simple bit. The caveat is price and the need for a stronger drill.
products.idealFor: Quart-size pots and small shrubs needing depth.
products.skipIf: You have a small drill or want the cheapest bit.

products.name: Insaga 2x9 Garden Auger
products.verdict: A 9 inch, 2 inch wide bit for seedlings, plugs and starter pots.
products.description:
Insaga is a 2 inch blade, 9 inches overall, with a 0.47 inch solid steel shaft, a 3/8 inch chuck fit and a 2.5 mm blade thickness. It is the smallest auger here.

It ranks last because it cannot make a hole for anything bigger than a plug or small starter pot, and 9 inches is shallow. It does fit any 3/8 inch chuck and is gentle on light drills, which suits seedling work where torque would tear up the soil.

Buy it for seedlings, plugs and small starter pots. The caveat is its small scale, so it will not handle a pot larger than a few inches.
products.idealFor: Seedlings, plugs and small starter pots.
products.skipIf: You plant anything above a few inches wide.

whatMatters.detail: The bit width sets the size of the hole, and it should match the root ball of the pot you plant. A 7 inch bit suits a gallon pot, while 3 inches suits bulbs and small plugs. Too narrow and you widen every hole by hand. Match the listed diameter to your largest pot, prefer slightly wider, and remember that a hole that is wider than the root ball is easy to backfill but one that is narrower is not.

Length is the working depth and also whether you can plant standing up. A 36 inch auger reaches deep and spares your back, while a 9 inch bit suits seedlings. Longer augers are harder to store and need a steadier hand on the drill. Check the stated length and match it to the depth your plants need, and keep in mind that the usable depth is a little less than the full length once the chuck is attached.

The hex or chuck size decides which drills fit. A 3/8 inch drive fits most cordless drills, while a 1/2 inch drive needs a bigger chuck. Wide bits in packed soil draw more torque, and the TCBWFY listing advises an 18V drill or more. Check the drive size on the listing before you order, and test that your chuck closes fully on the hex so the bit cannot slip under load.

Flighting is the spiral that lifts soil out of the hole, and thick steel keeps its shape in rocky or clay ground. Double 10-gauge flighting on the Power Planter is heavy duty, and a solid shaft resists twisting. Look for a stated gauge and a solid shaft, and avoid thin hollow bits, which bend the first time they meet a buried root or a stone in compacted ground.

A one-piece auger has no joint to loosen and transmits torque cleanly, while a detachable one packs smaller. The Jayzod separates for carrying but adds a joint that can flex. Choose one-piece if you plant at home and detachable if you travel or lack storage. Check how the sections lock together, and whether the joint is a pin or a threaded coupling, since that is the part that wears out first.

faq.q: Will these fit my cordless drill?
faq.a: Check the chuck. The VASGOR and Insaga fit a 3/8 inch chuck, while the Power Planter augers use a 1/2 inch hex. The TCBWFY needs a 3/8 inch chuck or larger and an 18V drill or greater.

faq.q: What mistake do gardeners make with augers?
faq.a: Choosing a bit too small for the pot. A 3 inch auger, such as the Jayzod or the Power Planter 3x36, only suits bulbs and plugs. For gallon pots, buy the 7 inch Power Planter so the root ball drops in.

faq.q: Is an auger worth it over a shovel?
faq.a: For many holes, yes. The Power Planter 7x28 bores a clean cylinder in seconds, while a shovel digs a ragged hole. For one or two plants a shovel is faster than fetching a drill.

faq.q: How should I use one safely?
faq.a: Start slowly, hold the drill with both hands and keep the bit vertical. If the bit snags on a root or rock, release the trigger at once. A 7 inch bit can twist the drill hard if it jams.

faq.q: How do I clean and store an auger?
faq.a: Knock off soil, rinse the flighting and dry it, then oil it lightly to prevent rust. The Jayzod's stainless shaft resists rust better than painted steel. Store the 36 inch Power Planter hung vertically.

faq.q: Can I use an auger in rocky ground?
faq.a: Poorly. Augers stall or kick back on rocks. The Power Planter's double 10-gauge flighting is heavy duty, but even it can jam. Probe the area first with a hand trowel, and move the hole if you hit stone.

finalTake: Buy the Power Planter 7x28 if you plant gallon-size shrubs and perennials: it is the only bit here wide enough, and it sits in the under $25 bucket. The VASGOR set suits mixed small-pot days, and the Power Planter 3x36 gives you reach for bulbs. The Jayzod is the detachable luxury, and the Insaga is strictly for seedlings.
